reconcile.connective: Defenders read Deuteronomy's prohibition as bounded to that moment — God shielded Moab when Israel was strong, but later turned the same nation over to judgment.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the inconsistency directly: God forbids Israel to distress Moab or take its land in Deuteronomy 2:9, yet Judges has Israel slay ten thousand Moabites and Jeremiah 48 calls for Moab to be cut off as a nation.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "How should the Moabites be treated?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), contradiction "How should the Moabites be treated?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: God would not suffer the Israelites, when they were the stronger, to distress the Moabites, nor give them any disturbance, though they were idolaters (Deu 2:9); yet now he suffered the Moabites to distress Israel, and strengthened them on purpose that they might …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Matthew Henry sets Deut 2:9 beside the later Moabite war and frames the shift as God's changing dispensation toward Moab — the core harmonizing move (the peace command was time-bound, not permanent).

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Deuteronomy 2:9
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly, harmonizing the prohibition as temporary: Israel was not to take Moab's land "at least not as yet, the measure of their sins not being fully up... otherwise in David's time they were subdued."
